paras: The Cowan saw mill shooting was a confrontation at Cowan, Tennessee, reported in early August 1881, in which a railroad employee named Northcutt and other armed hands from his train fired on about thirty Black men gathered at a saw mill. The Black men fled and no one was reported hurt. The only known account, printed by the Winchester Home Journal as "The Cowan Affair," came from a local informant and presented the shooting as Northcutt's defense against a threatened attack.

Cowan had a furnace and a saw mill along the railroad, and the Black men involved were described as coming "from the furnace." According to the informant, the trouble began in the store of Pattie & Shook in a quarrel between Northcutt, an employee of the Tennessee Coal & Railroad Company, and two Black men, "in which Northcutt got the best of it." The two men were said to have "threatened to have revenge."

In the informant's telling, about thirty Black men then gathered at the saw mill "with avowed intentions to mob Northcutt." Friends of Northcutt telegraphed him at Tracy to warn him, and he and the other hands on his train armed themselves. When the train reached the men waiting at the mill, the hands jumped off, advanced on them and fired several shots, which the account said were fired "without aiming to hurt them." The Black men fled to the furnace grounds, and the article closed with the words "This ended the affair."
No injuries were reported, and no report of arrests, charges or a court hearing appears in the coverage.

The episode appears in a single short item on page 3 of the Home Journal of Winchester, Tennessee, on August 3, 1881. The paper attributed its account to "one of the best citizens of the Cowan district" and printed it without comment, giving the Black men's intentions only as the informant described them. The item referred to the Black men throughout as "negroes," called the episode "the late row in Cowan," and named none of them. No other white paper's account and no Black-press account was found.

framing.detail: The Home Journal printed the informant's version without comment, casting the Black men as a would-be mob and the shooting as a warned man's defense that harmed no one.
